I actually disagree with some of the more recent reviews. Yes, the exams are now a lot more difficult than the past semesters, but I think Dr. Hirschauer provided us with a many resources to do well. Some of these resources included posted lecture videos (some of them were older but it was still on the same content), a beginner practice problem set, and then a more complex problem set for each chapter. Although she didn't provide any practice exams, I would say if you are 100% confident on the PP sets, you are bound to do at least decent on the exams. (80-90% range, and the averages were always low 60's%). - IMO Dr. Hirschauer is a nice and charismatic person, and her lectures were never boring to me. I also loved the Pokemon analogies (my childhood), but I can understand that she probably didn't include them as much since not everyone knows about it. I found her explanations to be very clear, and overall I can say that the resources she provided us, including the notes which were beautiful and organized, helped me to really learn the content. She was also always very available for office hours, despite the large amount of students in the class. - It was a bit frustrating not knowing the cutoffs, but that can't be helped since the curve is based on how well the class does/exam averages. I also think that the cutoffs are pretty high (as of now-> at least 83% is an A) but that might change a bit after finals (havent taken it yet). - there are some tricky details/part of problems on the exam that we never really went over in class (or ever), but honestly they only make up a few points anyway. I just felt that they were a bit unfair, but this isn't a major thing. - IMO the TA Praha wasn't bad, but during discussion his explanations were often unclear or sloppy(not thorough enough/missing details), and he goes through problems too fast sometimes. Also, his handwriting was super messy and it was strenuous to interpret anything he wrote during discussion. But he does seem to be very knowledgeable, and I think if you ask him questions after class or during office hours, he does a much better job of explaining things then. Also he is nice and I never felt uncomfortable approaching to ask for questions. Here are some tips for future students: 1. Keep up with the content. If you fall behind, it can be stressful to catch up (although not impossible). I personally was always behind, but once I caught up, I realized that if I had just reviewed or learned a little bit everyday, things would've been so much easier. 2. briefly review the content you will learn in lecture BEEFORE attending lecture. Even if it's just watching a youtube video without understanding what's going on, familiarizing yourself with the content will make understanding what's being taught during lecture much much easier. First time seeing the content -> familiarize. second time (lecture) -> learn. after lecture, review the notes, attempt the beginner sets provided, and watch other youtube videos if you need another perspective on the content. Ask TAs or got to office hours to clear up any complicated/confusing problems you encounter, or concepts. Do this for every chapter, before it's time for the next one. 3. Make sure you understand everything in the notes if you can. Even if it is a small detail, make sure you don't forget it, because on the exams there were often trickier problems that included those little details or exceptions, which is a main thing that contributed to exam difficulty. But obviously prioritize the "big picture" concepts first if you are on a time crunch. 4. DONT underestimate the amount of time you need to dedicate preparing for the exams. I spent several hours the week before exam week doing practice problems and reviewing/learning, but on the exam the questions always had these little things I was unsure about, and I would get points off here and there that added up to a LOT of points taken off. So start reviewing chapters you just learned as soon as possible, and I mean the day of or after you just went over it in lecture. This way you have time to get to really know the content, which is absolutely necessary for doing well. 5. do every practice problem provided and if you got something wrong, make a physical note of what you did wrong and why. If you dont know why, go back to the notes bcs the answer will be there 90% of the time. I really wish I did this from the start... 6. try to understand the reasoning behind every answer, dont just try to memorize patterns (unless specifically stated in lecture to memorize) because sometimes it depends on certain conditions and situations. This one is kinda hard to explain, but you might get what I mean after starting the semester. 7. Be sure you are able to complete problems quickly (but also dont rush, leading to careless mistakes). Exams had 15 problems with 1 hr 15 mins to complete...however, most of the problems took several minutes, esp the ones where you have to draw products or mechanisms. Basically, know the content well enough so that you are able to get through problems fast. Try timing yourself when doing practice problems, and if you notice the time is too long then think of ways/methods you can become more efficient. 8. test taking tip: during the exam, spend more time on problems you know you can get an answer to. If there is a concept you weren't able to study for and feel very unsure about, just put your best answer and dont spend too much time on it, because you will run out of/ waste a lot of time when you couldve used that time to complete other problems you are more likely to get right. the time goes by FAST and even when I studied a lot, I had to work really quickly just to complete all the problems before time was up. 9. If you are struggling to even start learning content, go to GSS because those problems are often simpler and can help you adjust. I was really impressed with the TAs Aubrey and Alice because they break things down in a way that even a little kid could understand. Overall, I would definitely recommend Dr. Hirschauer for Orgo 1. Just make sure to hit the ground running and try not to fall behind. For context I am an average student who procrastinates a lot but often manages to do well enough to get A's (might get a B in this class though, I just didn't take it as seriously as I should've). This class wasn't as bad as I thought it would be, especially since I was super terrified going in because people always say orgo is crazy difficult. But it's not really, it just requires a lot of time, and I even found it to be fun at times despite other frustrated moments. If you hate math and are more of a visual learner, you might like orgo I. So don't worry you'll be fine and you can do it :)

alright this man gets a 10/10 for personality but like a 6/10 for his teaching. class is super enjoyable because he is an entertaining little grandpa who just wants you to enjoy. the first test was mad easy and then they got progressively harder and but little was done to prepare us for the difference in difficulty. He was extremely nice and understanding this semester. Lectures could be a bit disorganized but he also has online recordings that cover all the material. Homeworks were tedious, but exams were quite easy and class average was very high.

First off, ignore my grade in this course. I genuinely did not put enough effort into the beginning of the semester and missed a number of lectures/homeworks because of it. The homeworks and exams are challenging to do, but they really test on your understanding of the material rather than just straight up memorizing facts and numbers. You can drop an exam, a hw, and a few quizzes. If you wanna be A- locked for orgo (especially if you're premed), I genuienly think the easiest professor to do that with is Koppel. I think she just has a bad rep cause people don't like her as a lab coordinator which is valid but as an orgo professor, she is actually really good. Her notes/lectures are pretty good, the discussion worksheets are such good practice, especially for the midterms, and her exams are extremely fair in my opinion. I don't wanna say they're easy cause it's orgo and no matter which professor you take, you're gonna have to put an insane amount of effort. But if you do your part, you will see that Koppel doesn't have any trick questions or any unexpected questions in her exams. Everything makes sense. On top of the exams, she has really easy homework, "quizzes" (they're online and graded on completion), and extra credit, that all together gives your grade a massive boost (8% boost for me). Also, her pass/fail cutoff is a 50% and she changes her cutoffs after every midterm based on the class average. For example, if the class average on midterm 1 is 62%, then 62% is the cutoff for C+/B-. By the third exam for my class, the B+/A- cutoff was a 76%. For Koppel, I think as long as you put in the effort to get at least 5% above the class average on every midterm, then you're pretty much B+/A- locked. I really think you should give Koppel a shot if you're torn about who to take for orgo, especially if you're trying to protect your GPA.

I found Orgo II with Dr. Davis to be much easier than Orgo I with Dr. Stocker. I loved Dr. Stocker as a professor, but Dr. Davis's exams were so much easier than hers. For synthesis problems or problems where you have to make the product, Dr. Davis often provides clues like the chemical formula that you can use to double-check your work. His exams are completely doable within the time limit; for the first exam, many people even finished 30 minutes early. He also drops the lowest exam and has 9 bonus points throughout the semester. Dr. Davis doesn't have any graded assignments other than the exams and bonus points, but he does post a lot of practice material. Make sure to complete the past exams he posts since they're really helpful for understanding the exam format. Some of the past exams even have a video of him going over the answers. He also posted readings and practice problems from the textbook, but I've never used them. Discussion was really helpful for nailing down the concepts from lecture. We did lots of practice problems, so I recommend going to them even though it's not required. As for lecture, Dr. Davis was a very engaging professor. He often inserts short examples of how the reactions are used in industry to synthesize different compounds. You don't have to memorize these, but they're sometimes referenced on exams. He's very thorough when explaining concepts and he posts his notes in case you miss anything. The only negative I can think of is that his teaching pace is somewhat variable. Sometimes he teaches so slow that I sit there for a few minutes doing nothing, whereas other times I'm scrambling to write everything down. My lecture time (12:30 pm) was also way behind the 8:00 am class since he frequently paused to take questions.

He is a nice guy but he barely speaks english and his lectures are so disorganized. His first test wasn't bad, but the second one was horrible and brought my grade down ten points. Nice person who seems to care. In class examples at times were hard to connect to homework questions. Reasonable exams and grading.

Decent teacher and lectures are easy to understand.
